draft.title: Government controls
card: War effort
In WWII the Australian government took wide powers to put the nation's people and resources behind the war. This effort is called total war.
Rationing
Some goods were limited so there was enough for the forces. Food such as tea, butter and meat, and clothing, were rationed. People used coupons to buy their share.
Censorship
The government controlled what newspapers and radio could report. News that might help the enemy or lower morale, such as ship losses or bombing damage, could be cut or changed.
Manpower direction
The government could direct people into jobs that the war needed, such as factory or farm work. It did this to supply the forces and the nation.
draft.remember: Rationing, censorship and directed work gave the government control of goods, news and labour.

a.q: Why did the government ration tea, butter and clothing in WWII?
opts: To make sure enough supplies were left for the war effort
To stop people from hearing news that could help the enemy
To move workers from their usual jobs into war industries
To raise money by taxing goods that people wanted most
a.why: Rationing limited how much each person could buy, so supplies were left for the forces and the war effort. Censorship is the control of news, not goods, so the second option describes a different control.
a.clue: Think about who else needed these goods.

b.q: In 1942 a newspaper in Brisbane is told it cannot print the details of a ship sunk near the coast. Which government control is this, and what is its main reason?
opts: Censorship, to keep news from the enemy and protect morale
Rationing, to save paper so supplies last for the forces
Manpower direction, to move journalists into war industries
Rationing, to make sure each person gets a fair news share
b.why: Stopping a paper from printing certain news is censorship. Its aim was to keep useful information from the enemy and to protect morale. Rationing limits goods bought with coupons, and the paper-saving option confuses a limit on goods with a limit on content.
b.clue: The government is controlling what is said, not what is bought.

a.best: To make sure enough supplies were left for the war effort

b.best: Censorship, to keep news from the enemy and protect morale

problems.detail: Why (a) says 'the second option' is censorship, but options are shown in random order. In the order given, the second option is the taxation one and the censorship option is third, so the reference can point to the wrong option. Name the option by its content instead.

The clue 'controlling what is said, not what is bought' rules out both rationing options and points straight to censorship, since manpower direction is plainly not about what is said. It nearly gives the answer away.
